name: Tongkat ali
lead: Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia, also called longjack or Malaysian ginseng) is a Southeast Asian shrub whose root is used in traditional medicine as an aphrodisiac and for fever, and is now sold worldwide as a dietary supplement marketed as a natural testosterone booster.[1][2][3] The roots contain quassinoids and alkaloids such as eurycomanone.[3]

In human research, a 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials found that E. longifolia supplementation was associated with higher serum total testosterone, with the authors noting a stronger effect in hypogonadal and aging men.[4] A 2024 systematic review of 27 proposed testosterone boosters concluded that most do not raise total testosterone against placebo, and counted E. longifolia among the agents assessed with three studies.[5] A meta-analysis of two randomised trials found no significant overall improvement in erectile function.[6]

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities it is discussed as a legal, low-risk supplement for testosterone, libido and training; members disagree on how large any effect is compared with testosterone replacement or anabolic steroids.[7][8][7]

paras: Eurycoma longifolia is a slow-growing evergreen shrub or small tree of the family Simaroubaceae, native to Southeast Asia including Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam. The root is the part used medicinally.[1] The common Malay name translates as 'Ali's walking stick', while Indonesian and Vietnamese names include pasak bumi and bach benh ('hundred ailments').[1]

Reviews of its traditional use list antimalarial, aphrodisiac, antidiabetic, antimicrobial and antipyretic applications, with decoctions made from roots, leaves and fruit for different complaints.[2][3]

In Southeast Asian folk medicine the plant has been used as an aphrodisiac and fever remedy, and a systematic review of its antimicrobial and antiparasitic activity links laboratory findings to its traditional use for jaundice and malaria.[1][2][9]

Standardised water-soluble root extracts, including branded products such as Physta (also sold as LJ100), are marketed for testosterone support, libido, energy and body composition.[1][4] A US-listed product label combines tongkat ali with chicken essence powder.[10]

The 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of five randomised trials reported a pooled standardised mean difference of 1.35 in total testosterone with E. longifolia, a significant increase, and said the benefit was confirmed in the hypogonadism subgroup.[4] The review included both healthy volunteers and men with low testosterone, and trials were small.[4]

A 2024 systematic review of 52 studies of 27 proposed testosterone boosters reported that most failed to increase total testosterone versus placebo; it included three E. longifolia studies and discussed E. longifolia, a pomegranate-cacao blend and a purified shilajit extract in its findings.[5]

A 6-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 45 men with androgen deficiency of aging males found erectile function improved in both interventions, with the best results in men combining 200 mg of E. longifolia with concurrent training.[11] A related randomised trial examined exercise with or without E. longifolia on strength and cardiorespiratory fitness in men with androgen deficiency.[12] A randomised trial in healthy young men examined effects on reproductive-hormone regulation.[13]

A 2015 meta-analysis of two randomised trials (139 participants) found no significant between-group difference overall in IIEF-5 at 12 weeks, with an improvement of about 2 points among those with lower baseline scores.[6] A separate randomised trial examined immune markers in middle-aged adults using a standardised extract.[14]

A 2010 review noted that although toxicity and safety evaluation studies had been carried out, a major gap remained in the scientific basis for commercial use and consumer safety clearance of tongkat ali products.[2] A randomised pharmacokinetic study reported that an E. longifolia water extract modified propranolol bioavailability, indicating the potential for interaction with some drugs.[15] A New Zealand primary-care article on tongkat ali (long jack) is also available.[16] The sources reviewed do not provide a comprehensive adverse-event profile.

The proposed mechanisms are largely from animal and laboratory work. Standardised quassinoid-rich extracts improved spermatogenesis and fertility in male rats via the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, and eurycomanone has been reported to inhibit phosphodiesterase and aromatase activity in steroidogenesis.[17][18] Human trial authors suggest testosterone increases may arise from activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal and/or adrenal axes, mainly in older adults and nonhealthy populations.[13] A 2012 paper asked whether a standardised extract could be a testosterone booster for late-onset hypogonadism.[19]

Tongkat ali has been sold in the bodybuilding supplement market since at least the early 2000s, when T Nation advertised a product containing pharmaceutical-grade E. longifolia.[20] On looksmax.org, threads ask whether it lowers or raises DHT, whether it is 'cope' compared with SARMs or steroids, and promote it as 'backed by studies'.[7][8][21]

Human studies include a 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials on total testosterone,[4] a 2024 systematic review of testosterone boosters,[5] a 2015 meta-analysis on erectile function,[6] a 6-month randomised trial in androgen-deficient men,[11] a randomised trial of exercise with or without E. longifolia on strength and fitness,[12] a randomised trial in healthy young men,[13] a randomised immunomodulation trial,[14] and a pharmacokinetic interaction trial with propranolol.[15] Registered trials include an erectile-dysfunction study of a tongkat ali plus maca product (n=197) and a small intimacy study.[22] Animal studies include libido and semen work in boars and sleep consolidation in mice.[23][24]

lore.intro: Tongkat ali is a staple of 'natural test' stacks on looksmax.org and T Nation. Discussion ranges from enthusiastic summaries of trials to scepticism about whether any legal supplement matters.[7][8][21]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org post says studies show it increases total and free testosterone by lowering SHBG and cites a 200 mg/day trial reporting about a 37 percent rise.[8]
claims.experts: A 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials reported a significant pooled increase in total testosterone, strongest in hypogonadal and aging men, while a 2024 review of 27 boosters found most do not raise total testosterone.[4][5]

claims.claim: Tongkat ali improves libido and erectile function
claims.believers: Forum posts and supplement marketing describe it as an aphrodisiac and energy aid, in line with its traditional reputation.[8][20]
claims.experts: A 2015 meta-analysis of two trials found no significant overall improvement in IIEF-5 at 12 weeks, though men with lower baseline scores improved, and a 6-month trial in men with androgen deficiency reported better erectile function with E. longifolia plus training.[6][11]

claims.claim: Tongkat ali lowers cortisol and improves body composition
claims.believers: The same looksmax.org post says modern research backs reduced cortisol and improved body composition.[8]
claims.experts: A randomised trial examined effects on strength and cardiorespiratory fitness in androgen-deficient men, and a trial in healthy young men examined hormone regulation; the sources reviewed do not give pooled results for cortisol or body composition.[12][13]

claims.claim: Natural testosterone from tongkat ali rivals or beats injected testosterone
claims.believers: One looksmax.org reply asserts that '1000 ng/dl natural testosterone mogs any amount of synthetic testosterone'; another says any legal supplement has negligible results on its own.[8][7]
claims.experts: No published trial has compared tongkat ali with testosterone replacement or anabolic steroids; the 2024 review concluded most testosterone boosters fail to raise total testosterone.[5]

card.summary: Southeast Asian root extract sold as a 'natural test booster'; small trials lean positive, but broader reviews are sceptical.
card.aka: Eurycoma longifolia; longjack; Malaysian ginseng; LJ100
card.note: Trials are small and results differ between reviews; one study found it altered propranolol bioavailability.

quick.overview:
Tongkat ali is a Southeast Asian root used traditionally as an aphrodisiac and now sold as a testosterone-support supplement. It is popular in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles.

A 2022 meta-analysis of small randomised trials found higher total testosterone with E. longifolia, especially in men with low levels, but a 2024 review of 27 testosterone boosters concluded most do not raise total testosterone, and erectile-function results are mixed.
quick.mechanism: Lab and rat studies suggest its quassinoids act on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and on steroidogenic enzymes; forum posts also claim it lowers SHBG, which the sources reviewed do not confirm.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited; a 2010 review noted gaps in safety evidence for commercial products, and one study found a water extract changed propranolol absorption. It is sold as a supplement, so product content varies.
